# SaaS Hiring Benchmarks 2026: Time-to-Fill, Cost & Attrition

The era of growth-at-all-costs hiring in software is officially behind us. Between 2020 and 2022, enterprise and mid-market SaaS companies operated on a simple mandate: acquire headcount to capture market share. Revenue multiples rewarded top-line expansion above all else, leading talent acquisition (TA) leaders to build large, high-velocity recruiting engines capable of processing thousands of candidates a month.

By 2024, the market abruptly recalibrated. Cash preservation, net revenue retention (NRR), and path to profitability replaced gross seat additions as the core metrics evaluated by board boards and venture partners. As we operate in 2026, the SaaS hiring ecosystem has settled into a disciplined, operationally rigorous equilibrium. The "Rule of 40" now dictates headcount planning. CHROs and VPs of Talent are held to the same financial and operational rigor as supply chain leaders or revenue operations directors.

To run a modern SaaS recruiting engine efficiently, talent leaders cannot rely on generic, cross-industry hiring data. A standard Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) or Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) average aggregates retail, hospitality, manufacturing, and traditional enterprise IT. Those figures obscure the realities of software recruitment—such as technical screening drop-offs, equity compensation scrutiny, and hyper-specialized go-to-market (GTM) skill sets.

This report translates broader industry data from SHRM, LinkedIn, and the BLS into specific, operational benchmarks for mid-market and enterprise SaaS companies. Whether you are scaling a remote engineering group across secondary tech hubs like Charlotte and Salt Lake City, or rebuilding a high-performing quota-bearing sales team in Austin, these operational benchmarks provide the baseline required to audit your TA organization, align hiring managers, and execute against your 2026 plan.

---

## 1. Time-to-Fill by Role & Seniority: The Realities of SaaS Capacity Planning

Time-to-fill—measured from the date a requisition receives formal finance approval to the date a candidate signs an offer letter—remains the primary metric for operational alignment between TA and business leaders. However, treating time-to-fill as a singular, company-wide average creates systematic planning errors. 

In SaaS, time-to-fill varies dramatically across functional pillars (GTM vs. Product & Engineering) and seniority levels. A blanket 45-day target leads to overstaffed sales teams sitting without engineering support, or executive searches dragging on long enough to derail product roadmaps.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                  2026 SaaS Time-to-Fill Ranges                    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| SDR / BDR                         | 28 - 35 Days                  |
| Customer Success Manager (Mid)    | 35 - 45 Days                  |
| Mid-Market Account Executive      | 42 - 52 Days                  |
| Senior Staff Software Engineer    | 60 - 75 Days                  |
| VP of Product / Engineering       | 90 - 120 Days                 |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Functional Role Breakdowns

#### Go-To-Market (GTM) Roles
*   **Sales Development Representatives (SDRs / BDRs):** **28 – 35 days.** Sourcing volume for outbound SDRs remains high, but screening criteria have shifted from raw activity metrics to written communication skill, AI-assisted prospecting capabilities, and business acumen.
*   **Mid-Market Account Executives (AEs):** **42 – 52 days.** Finding reps with proven track records in selling complex, multi-stakeholder SaaS solutions requires rigorous historical performance verification. 
*   **Enterprise AEs:** **55 – 70 days.** Enterprise reps managing six-figure ACV deals require deep vertical knowledge and long-cycle sales execution. Interview loops often stall at the custom presentation or mock discovery stage.

#### Product & Engineering Roles
*   **Full-Stack / Backend Engineers (Mid-Senior):** **45 – 60 days.** Sourcing activity is dense, but pass-rates at the technical assessment phase (e.g., HackerRank or live architecture reviews) frequently fall below 15%.
*   **Staff & Principal Engineers:** **60 – 75 days.** High compensation expectations combined with equity liquidity concerns keep passive talent anchored at established platforms unless presented with exceptionally clear technical scope.
*   **Product Managers (Senior / Group PM):** **50 – 65 days.** SaaS companies have tightened product management profiles, moving away from generalist coordinators toward domain experts with proven unit-economics and PLG (product-led growth) experience.

#### Leadership & Executive Search
*   **VP / C-Suite (Product, Engineering, Sales):** **90 – 120 days.** Executive loops in 2026 require extensive board alignment, candidate background auditing, and compensation structuring around performance-based equity milestones.

> **Benchmark:** Across all mid-market and enterprise SaaS roles, the median time-to-fill stands at **52 days**. However, top-quartile TA teams keep GTM roles under **38 days** and technical roles under **48 days** by enforcing strict SLAs on hiring manager scorecard submissions and interview scheduling.

### The Impact of Regional Hubs on Time-to-Fill

Geographic distribution strategies directly influence search duration. While fully remote roles generate high inbound application volume, they incur an operational tax during resume triage. Conversely, hybrid mandates in emerging tech hubs exhibit distinct cycle times:

```
                  TIME-TO-FILL BY GEOGRAPHIC REGION
┌──────────────────┬───────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│ Region / Hub     │ Average Time-to-Fill  │ Key Talent Dynamics      │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Austin, TX       │ 44 Days (GTM Focus)   │ Dense sales talent pool; │
│                  │                       │ high competition for AE  │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Salt Lake City   │ 41 Days (SDR/CSM)     │ High-volume GTM engine;  │
│ / Silicon Slopes │                       │ efficient phone screens  │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Charlotte &      │ 52 Days (Fintech/Eng) │ Maturing engineering     │
│ Raleigh, NC      │                       │ talent; steady supply    │
├──────────────────┼───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Bay Area & NYC   │ 62 Days (Core Tech)   │ Ultra-competitive; high  │
│                  │                       │ counter-offer rates      │
└──────────────────┴───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
```

*   **Austin, TX & Salt Lake City, UT:** GTM roles fill approximately 10–15% faster in these markets compared to national averages due to high concentrations of experienced SaaS sales representatives and localized sales enablement talent pools.
*   **Raleigh-Durham & Charlotte, NC:** Engineering roles in the Research Triangle and Charlotte financial-tech corridors show consistent, stable candidate movement. Time-to-fill for senior infrastructure and security roles averages **52 days**, benefiting from lower voluntary attrition rates than legacy coastal hubs.
*   **Bay Area & New York Metropolitan Area:** High candidate selectivity and frequent counter-offers push technical time-to-fill to **62+ days**, even for mid-stage software firms offering competitive cash packages.

## 2. Real Cost-per-Hire: Direct Costs vs. Fully Loaded Realities

Cost-per-hire (CPH) is often reported as a simple calculation: total external recruitment spend divided by total hires. This shallow reporting masks the true economic impact of candidate acquisition on a SaaS business. 

To provide actionable financial data, CPH must be broken into **Direct Operational Costs** (agency fees, sourcing tools, job boards) and **Fully Loaded Costs** (internal recruiter cash compensation, hiring manager interview hours, ATS/tech stack overhead, and candidate travel/reimbursement).

### The Math Behind SaaS Cost-Per-Hire

```
   Fully Loaded Sourcing Cost + Recruiter Overhead + Tech Stack + Agency Fees
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
                             Total Hires in Period
```

For a 250-person SaaS company making 40 hires per year, the cost profile breaks down across three distinct categories:

```
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       Fully Loaded Cost-per-Hire Breakdown                      |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Cost Component                 | Non-Technical Role      | Senior Technical Role|
+--------------------------------+-------------------------+----------------------+
| Internal Recruiter Time (Alloc)| $1,800                  | $3,200               |
| Hiring Manager/Team Hours      | $1,400 (12 hrs total)   | $2,800 (18 hrs total)|
| TA Tech Stack Allocation       | $650                    | $650                 |
| Sourcing & Job Board Spend     | $450                    | $1,200               |
| Agency / Search Partner Fees   | $0 (In-house core)      | $18,000 (20% fee)    |
| Assessment & Background Checks | $150                    | $350                 |
+--------------------------------+-------------------------+----------------------+
| TOTAL FULLY LOADED COST        | $4,450                  | $26,200              |
+--------------------------------+-------------------------+----------------------+
```

### Expense Categories Explained

#### 1. Internal Recruiting Allocation
The fully burdened salary, benefits, and bonus of the internal TA team. In 2026, an in-house Senior Tech Recruiter in a market like Denver or Atlanta commands a base salary of $120,000–$145,000, with total burdened cost reaching $160,000–$185,000. If that recruiter closes 18 technical hires a year, the internal labor allocation alone is roughly **$9,400 to $10,200 per hire**.

#### 2. The TA Tech Stack Tax
SaaS TA organizations utilize specialized software stacks to maintain efficiency. The cost per recruiter desk typically ranges between **$4,000 and $7,500 annually**, incorporating:
*   **Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS):** Ashby, Greenhouse, or Lever ($12,000–$40,000 platform fee depending on headcount).
*   **Outbound Sourcing Tools:** LinkedIn Recruiter Enterprise ($9,200/seat/year), Gem, or Instahyre.
*   **Interview Intelligence & Screening:** Metaview, BrightHire, HackerRank, or TestGorilla ($3,000–$12,000 annually).

#### 3. Search Partner & Contingency Agency Spend
When internal capacity breaches capacity limits or specialized executive talent is required, agency placement fees add significant capital outlay. Standard SaaS contingency placement fees sit between **18% and 25%** of first-year base salary. 

For an Enterprise AE with a $160,000 base salary, a 20% placement fee equals **$32,000** in direct, non-recurring external expense.

> **Benchmark:** The broad SHRM baseline places general cost-per-hire around **$4,700**. In SaaS, the overall fully loaded average is **$7,800 for non-technical roles** and **$22,500 for specialized technical or mid-level management roles**. When relying on third-party contingency search firms, technical cost-per-hire frequently exceeds **$35,000**.

## 3. Offer Acceptance Rates: Winning Passive Talent in a Pragmatic Market

The offer acceptance rate (OAR)—calculated as total accepted written offers divided by total extended written offers—is a direct indicator of brand strength, market-competitive compensation alignment, and candidate experience velocity.

In 2026, candidates prioritize cash security, clear path to quota, and realistic hybrid expectations over abstract equity promises or speculative perks.

```
                      2026 SaaS Offer Acceptance Rates
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Target Benchmark Range                                    82% - 88%    │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ High-Performing TA Teams (Clear comp, rapid loops)         > 90%       │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Underperforming Teams (Slow debriefs, equity heavy)        < 72%       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

When offer acceptance rates drop below 75%, it signal systemic issues in the talent acquisition operational pipeline:
1.  **Compensation Misalignment:** Extending offers based on out-of-date 2022 market rates or over-leveraged commission structures.
2.  **Extended Loop Duration:** Taking longer than 48 hours between the final panel interview and extending a verbal offer, allowing competitors to intervene.
3.  **Equity Valuation Skepticism:** Candidates discounting illiquid stock options or RSUs in un-budgeted or down-round environments.

### The Mechanics of Offer Rejections

To understand why candidates decline offers in modern software environments, consider this real-world scenario from a mid-market SaaS infrastructure firm based in Austin, Texas:

> #### Field Anecdote: The Cost of Inflexible RTO Policies
>
> A 300-person B2B SaaS company in Austin extended an offer to a Senior Cloud Infrastructure Engineer. The package matched market benchmarks: $175,000 base salary, a standard 10% annual bonus, and equity options. 
> 
> However, during the final approval stage, the executive leadership team insisted on adding a strict "3-day per week in-office" clause for their downtown Austin office. The candidate—who lived in Round Rock, TX, and had communicated a preference for a hybrid model capped at 1 day per week—rejected the offer within 24 hours. 
> 
> The company spent another 41 days searching for a replacement, eventually settling on a less experienced candidate who required an extra $15,000 in base salary to offset the daily commute. The direct cost of that single rejected offer exceeded $18,000 in lost engineering sprint capacity and additional recruiting cycles.

```
                     PRIMARY CAUSES OF OFFER DECLINES
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│ Primary Decline Reason                   │ Frequency Share          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Base Cash Compensation Below Market      │ 34%                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Commute / Restrictive RTO Mandates       │ 26%                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Counter-Offer from Existing Employer     │ 18%                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Unrealistic Sales Quotas / Low OTE Split │ 14%                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Role Scope / Career Path Ambiguity       │ 8%                       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
```

### Maximizing Acceptance Velocity

Top-performing SaaS talent functions maintain offer acceptance rates above **85%** by instituting three specific operational standards:

1.  **Pre-Closing at Stage Three:** The recruiter verifies compensation expectations, notice periods, counter-offer likelihood, and decision-making criteria *before* the candidate enters the final executive interview loop.
2.  **The 24-Hour Verbal Extension:** Verbal offers are extended within 24 hours of panel completion. Formal written agreements via DocuSign follow within 12 business hours.
3.  **Executive Connection:** The hiring manager and functional executive schedule a 15-minute informal call within 48 hours of offer receipt to walk through team roadmaps, target territory allocations, and organizational support structures.

## 4. Source-of-Hire Mix: Quality vs. Volume in Modern Pipelines

The channels through which SaaS hires are generated have fundamentally shifted. Between 2018 and 2021, inbound job board postings accounted for a massive percentage of overall hires. In 2026, the rise of automated job application scripts, AI-generated resumes, and automated mass-apply platforms has flooded ATS pipelines with unqualified applicants.

As a result, inbound application volume has decoupled from hire volume. A job post for a remote Customer Success Manager may receive 1,200 inbound applications within 72 hours, yet yield fewer than 3 candidates who pass the preliminary phone screen.

```
              SOURCE-OF-HIRE PIPELINE DISTRIBUTION (2026)
┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
│ Sourcing Channel        │ % of Total Pipeline  │ % of Final Hires   │
├─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
│ Outbound Passive Sourcing│ 25%                  │ 42%                │
├─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
│ Employee Referrals      │ 12%                  │ 28%                │
├─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
│ Inbound Applications    │ 55%                  │ 16%                │
├─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
│ Specialized Partners    │ 8%                   │ 14%                │
└─────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴────────────────────┘
```

### Channel Breakdown and ROI Analysis

#### 1. Outbound Passive Sourcing (42% of Hires)
Direct outreach via specialized tools (LinkedIn Recruiter, Gem, GitHub, customized sourcing engines) remains the primary engine for high-intent SaaS hiring. 

*   **Operational Metric:** Response rates for outbound messages have dropped globally from ~25% in 2021 to **8% – 14%** in 2026. 
*   **Tactical Fix:** Recruiters using hyper-personalized outreach based on specific code commits, deal size achievements, or clear career path progression achieve reply rates exceeding **22%**.

#### 2. Employee Referrals (28% of Hires)
Employee referral programs remain the highest-ROI talent channel, delivering the lowest time-to-fill (median **29 days**) and highest 12-month retention rates.

*   **Operational Metric:** Leading software firms target **25% – 35%** of total hires via referral channels.
*   **Tactical Fix:** Payout structures have evolved. Instead of paying a flat $2,000 bonus at 90 days, companies tier payments: $1,000 on the hire's start date and $2,500 at their 180-day milestone for critical technical or quota-bearing roles.

#### 3. Inbound Applications (16% of Hires)
While generating over half of total ATS application volume, inbound job postings account for less than a fifth of actual hires. 

*   **Operational Metric:** The qualification rate of inbound SaaS applications currently sits between **1.5% and 3.5%**.
*   **Tactical Fix:** Implementing automated screening questions in platforms like Ashby or Greenhouse—requiring candidates to verify location eligibility, specific tech stack experience, or compensation ranges—eliminates 80% of unviable applicants automatically.

#### 4. Specialized Talent Partners & Niche Search (14% of Hires)
Third-party talent partners, specialized embedded recruiting teams, and executive search boutiques fill critical pipeline gaps when internal teams run out of capacity or lack localized candidate networks.

*   **Operational Metric:** External partners drive high conversion rates, with **1 out of every 3 submitted candidates** reaching the final interview loop when briefed correctly.

## 5. The 90-Day Attrition Crisis: Root Causes and Preventive Ops

Early attrition—defined as voluntary or involuntary candidate departure within the first 90 days of employment—is one of the most expensive operational failures in a software enterprise. 

When a candidate leaves within three months, the business loses:
1.  The fully loaded cost-per-hire spent acquiring the employee ($8,000 – $35,000+).
2.  The fully burdened cash compensation paid during onboarding ($20,000 – $45,000).
3.  The management bandwidth spent training and onboarding the individual.
4.  The opportunity cost of vacant territorial coverage or delayed product development.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|               SaaS Early Attrition Benchmarks (0-90 Days)        |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Healthy Benchmark Range           | 3% - 5%                       |
| Industry Average                  | 8% - 12%                      |
| High-Risk / Broken Onboarding     | > 15%                         |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### The Drivers of Early Attrition in SaaS

Why do tech hires fail in their first 90 days? Data collected across exit interviews and 30-day onboarding check-ins reveals three recurring causes:

```
                  ROOT CAUSES OF 90-DAY ATTRITION
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│ Failure Category                         │ Primary Symptom          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Quota & Territory Misrepresentation      │ Sales reps discover      │
│                                          │ targets are unachievable │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Technical Scope Inflation                │ Engineers find stack is  │
│                                          │ burdened by legacy debt  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Onboarding & Enablement Breakdown        │ Lack of documentation;   │
│                                          │ absent hiring manager    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
```

#### 1. Quota & Territory Misrepresentation (Sales Roles)
The single largest driver of early turnover in revenue organizations is the disconnect between interview promises and operational reality. When an Account Executive arrives and discovers that 80% of the sales team is missing quota, or that their assigned territory consists entirely of cold, un-worked SMB accounts rather than warm mid-market leads, trust breaks down instantly.

#### 2. Technical Scope Inflation (Engineering Roles)
Engineers hired under the promise of building new greenfield architecture often find themselves assigned exclusively to technical debt, legacy bug resolution, or undocumented maintenance tasks. If the interview process misrepresents the state of the codebase, developer churn spike within the first 60 days.

#### 3. Onboarding & Enablement Breakdown
In remote and hybrid work environments, onboarding cannot happen by osmosis. If a new Customer Success Manager spends their first two weeks waiting for system access permissions, hardware shipments, or updated product documentation, their engagement drops precipitously.

### Field Anecdote: The Salt Lake City SDR Cohort

> #### Field Anecdote: Fixing Quota Misalignment
>
> A growing Series B SaaS company located in Silicon Slopes (Salt Lake City area) hired a cohort of six SDRs to power a new enterprise outbound motion. During the recruiting process, candidates were told the average ramp time was 30 days, with standard commission payouts expected in Month Two.
> 
> In reality, the company’s product lacked necessary integration docs for enterprise clients, extending the actual sales cycle from 45 days to 110 days. By day 75, four of the six SDRs had missed their quota tiers, received zero commission payouts, and felt misled regarding team performance. 
> 
> Three of them resigned within two weeks of each other, taking jobs at competing software firms down the street. The company was forced to write off over **$75,000 in onboarding and salary investments**, while spending another two months backfilling the roles.
> 
> The structural fix required aligning the TA team with Sales Ops to update job specs with realistic 90-day onboarding milestones and extending the commission draw period to 90 days. Subsequent cohort attrition dropped to zero.

## 6. Operationalizing Talent Acquisition for Efficiency in 2026

To operate at enterprise standards, CHROs and TA leaders must convert recruiting from a reactive service provider into a predictable operational discipline. This requires setting firm Service Level Agreements (SLAs) across the candidate pipeline and establishing rigid funnel conversion metrics.

### Stage-by-Stage Funnel Conversion Benchmarks

A healthy recruiting funnel follows precise conversion ratios. Tracking these stage-by-stage conversions allows TA leaders to pinpoint exactly where pipeline drop-offs occur.

```
       CANDIDATE FUNNEL CONVERSION BENCHMARKS
  
  [Sourced Candidates / Inbound Applicants]
                     │
                     ▼ (15% - 20% Pass)
          [Recruiter Phone Screen]
                     │
                     ▼ (50% - 60% Pass)
          [Hiring Manager Screen]
                     │
                     ▼ (40% - 50% Pass)
        [Technical / Practical Loop]
                     │
                     ▼ (25% - 35% Pass)
             [Final Panel / Debrief]
                     │
                     ▼ (80% - 85% Pass)
            [Offer Extended]
                     │
                     ▼ (82% - 88% Accept)
             [Hired Candidate]
```

#### Detailed Stage Thresholds

1.  **Top of Funnel to Recruiter Screen:** **15% – 20%** of sourced passive candidates convert to a scheduled screen. For inbound applicants, this number drops to **2% – 4%**.
2.  **Recruiter Screen to Hiring Manager Screen:** **50% – 60%**. If your recruiters pass more than 70% of candidates to the hiring manager, your initial qualification bar is likely too low. If they pass fewer than 40%, the recruiter and hiring manager are misaligned on core job criteria.
3.  **Hiring Manager Screen to Technical Assessment / Practical Loop:** **40% – 50%**. The hiring manager should filter out candidates lacking functional experience before wasting team resources on extensive panel loops.
4.  **Technical Loop to Final Panel:** **25% – 35%**. Technical assessments should be rigorous enough to filter out non-performers, but not so tedious that qualified candidates withdraw from the process.
5.  **Final Panel to Offer Extended:** **25% – 30%**. If a team interviews four final-round candidates and none receive an offer, the previous loop stages are failing to filter correctly.
6.  **Offer Extended to Offer Accepted:** **82% – 88%**. 

### Standardizing Hiring SLAs

To hit target time-to-fill and lower fully loaded cost-per-hire, TA teams must contractually agree on operational SLAs with functional business units:

```
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         SaaS Recruitment SLA Directives                         |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Pipeline Stage                 | Operational SLA Limit  | Responsible Party     |
+--------------------------------+------------------------+-----------------------+
| Requisition Approval to Kickoff| Within 48 Hours        | TA Lead + Hiring Mgr  |
| Inbound Resume Review          | Within 72 Hours        | Recruiter             |
| Recruiter Screen Feedback      | Within 24 Hours        | Recruiter             |
| Hiring Manager Interview Feedback| Within 24 Hours      | Hiring Manager        |
| Final Panel Scorecard Submission| Within 12 Hours       | Interview Panel       |
| Post-Panel Debrief Call        | Within 24 Hours        | Full Interview Team   |
| Offer Extension                | Within 24 Hours (Verbal)| Recruiter + VP      |
+--------------------------------+------------------------+-----------------------+
```

> **Benchmark:** Companies that enforce a strict **24-hour SLA** on interview scorecard submissions shorten their overall hiring cycle by **11 days** on average and improve offer acceptance rates by **7%**, as high-caliber candidates view fast feedback as a reflection of high operational standards.

## 7. Operational Benchmark Summary Checklist

Use this checklist during executive staff reviews or quarterly talent audits to evaluate your talent acquisition platform against enterprise standards:

### 1. Speed & Velocity
* [ ] Is your overall company-wide median time-to-fill under **52 days**?
* [ ] Do critical GTM roles (SDR, MM AE) close within **30 to 45 days**?
* [ ] Are candidates moving from initial screen to offer within **21 calendar days**?

### 2. Financial Precision
* [ ] Do you track **Fully Loaded Cost-Per-Hire**, including recruiter compensation, manager hours, and tech stack spend?
* [ ] Is your internal fully loaded CPH kept under **$8,000 for non-technical roles** and **$18,000 for technical roles**?
* [ ] Is third-party contingency agency spend capped at less than **15%** of overall hiring volume?

### 3. Pipeline Quality & Retention
* [ ] Is your offer acceptance rate standing firmly between **82% and 88%**?
* [ ] Does direct outbound sourcing and employee referrals generate more than **60%** of your total hires?
* [ ] Is your early 90-day attrition rate below **5%** across all business units?

### 4. Operational Alignment
* [ ] Do hiring managers submit interview scorecards within **24 hours** of completing candidate screens?
* [ ] Are offer letters extended within **24 hours** of final debrief sign-offs?
* [ ] Are sales quotas, target territories, and codebase debt communicated transparently during candidate loops to prevent onboarding churn?
